title: Fukuoka — ramen
body:
Shin Shin, Tenjin main store — 3-2-19 Tenjin, Chuo-ku (092-732-4006), 30 seats. The locals' pick: an independent Fukuoka ranking of local ramen put it #1, ahead of the globally famous chains. ≈11:00–03:00 (last order 02:30) — genuinely one of the few well-regarded shops open past midnight, a good late-night stop after Tenjin yatai. Closed day is disputed across sources (3rd Tuesday vs. Wednesday) — confirm on arrival. Walk-in/queue; third-party platforms show a reservation option for this location, worth a call ahead for a specific night. How: short walk from Tenjin Station.

Ganso Nagahamaya — 2-5-25 Nagahama, Chuo-ku, Trust Park Nagahama 3-1F (092-711-8154). The actual 1952 originator of Nagahama-style tonkotsu ramen, not one of the many shops that later took the name. Open 5:00–1:45am, closed only Dec 31–Jan 5 — the early open makes it a genuine post-yatai or early-morning option. Single-item menu (broth strength/noodle firmness/scallion only), walk-in/counter only. How: near the Nagahama fish-market area, a short taxi or bus from Tenjin/Hakata rather than a direct subway walk.

Honest note on the famous names: Ichiran and Ippudo are both HQ'd in Fukuoka and world-famous, but local sentiment (a personal local blogger's ranked top-10 explicitly excludes both as "overpriced," and multiple Q&A threads call them "sousaku" ramen outside Hakata's traditional lineages, largely ignored by residents) points elsewhere. Ichiran in particular draws a real queue at almost any hour, reportedly even before noon — mostly tourists. Worth a look at Ippudo's original 1985 Daimyo shop for the history if you're curious, but Shin Shin and Ganso Nagahamaya are the better bowls by local reckoning.

title: Fukuoka — yatai, motsunabe & mentaiko
body:
Yatai (street stalls): officially licensed and location-assigned by Fukuoka City, concentrated in Tenjin and Nakasu. Both matter, for different reasons: local sentiment (a Fukuoka-local blog explicitly asking "is it true locals don't go to Fukuoka's yatai?") is clear that Tenjin is where residents actually eat — cheaper (≈¥100–200 less per ramen bowl), more Hakata-ben than tourist chatter — while Nakasu is the livelier, more tourist-facing riverside scene, worth seeing for the atmosphere even if Tenjin is the better meal. Both run ≈18:00 to the small hours; best windows are right at opening or ≈21:00 once the first dinner rush clears. Bring ¥1,000 notes — ~90% cash-only, and stalls often can't break a ¥10,000 bill.

Motsunabe (offal hot pot): Maedaya is the local-favorite pick — it recurs independently across a Q&A thread, a 2026 locals' ranking, and a resident magazine mention, a stronger convergence than any single other option found. Ganso Motsunabe Rakutenchi, Tenjin Honten (B2F ACROS Fukuoka, 1-1-1 Tenjin — 092-741-2746, 11:00–22:00, food/drink L.O. 21:30, 5 min from Tenjin Station Exit 16) is the famous, easily bookable alternative — online reservations run through its own site, useful if you want it locked in rather than a walk-in gamble; local rankings still place it a respectable 3rd for flavor, so it isn't a pure tourist trap, just the bigger, easier-to-book name.

Mentaiko (spicy cod roe): buy at Fukuya's Nakasu Honten (2-6-10 Nakasu, Hakata-ku — Mon–Fri 9:00–22:00, weekends/holidays 9:30–18:00, no closed days) — Fukuya is the brand that invented commercial mentaiko, and this location stocks a honten-exclusive tin (≈¥3,672) not sold elsewhere. To eat it mentaiko-forward, Kisuimaru inside Hakata 1-Bangai / JR Hakata City (B1F, 7:30–23:00, breakfast menu 7:30–10:00 with all-you-can-eat mentaiko/rice/miso soup) sits right at Hakata Station — zero transit cost, a strong early-departure-day option. Disproved claim, worth flagging so it doesn't creep back in from a generic source: there is no "Mentai Park" (Kanefuku's mentaiko theme-park chain) anywhere in Fukuoka Prefecture, despite this being a commonly repeated claim — checked directly against Kanefuku's own site; its six locations are all elsewhere in Japan.

title: Fukuoka — Yanagibashi Market & a Dazaifu-day ramen stop
body:
Yanagibashi Rengo Ichiba — nicknamed "Fukuoka's Kitchen," a genuine working public fish/produce market with small sit-down counters, off the standard Hakata/Tenjin/Nakasu circuit that repeat visitors have likely already covered. Fukuoka Now, the city's long-running resident/expat magazine, has independently featured it across multiple years as one of the city's most distinctive spots for a visitor to see actual daily commerce rather than a tourist market. ⚠ Check current hours before going — traditional fish markets often skip Sundays, and this pass didn't independently re-confirm today's exact schedule.

On the Dazaifu day trip (see Sights), swing back through Nagahama for Ganso Nagahamaya (above) rather than eating near the shrine itself — Dazaifu's approach street is built for the grilled-mochi souvenir crowd, not a real meal.

title: Sapporo — jingisukan, miso ramen & Nijo Market
body:
Jingisukan Daruma Honten, Susukino — Sapporo's signature charcoal-grilled lamb, done as a shared, drinking-friendly grill format that suits a celebration dinner better than a solo ramen counter. Founded 1954, its own sauce recipe, named as "the place" for jingisukan across multiple independent write-ups. ⚠ Address/hours corroborated across three independent sources but not fetched directly from an official page this pass — call ahead to book for two and confirm current hours, especially if using it for the Oct 24 birthday dinner. Sapporo Beer Garden is the larger, more tour-group-scaled alternative if Daruma is full.

Miso ramen: Sapporo is the birthplace of miso ramen; Menya Saimi stood out in this research as having genuine local following (its recipe became a retail instant-ramen product) rather than just tourist-guide visibility — a single-source lead, worth a walk-by rather than a locked plan.

Nijo Market — Sapporo's classic seafood market, good for a morning uni/crab breakfast; this pass didn't find a strong "locals go elsewhere instead" alternative, so treat it as the standard, reasonably reliable pick rather than a discovered secret.

title: Sendai — gyutan, hiyashi chūka & the back-alley izakaya lanes
body:
Ryūtei — the actual restaurant where hiyashi chūka (cold ramen) was invented in 1937, adapting the Shanghainese dish liangbanmian; independently confirmed via its Wikipedia origin entry and a named local food blogger's own recommendation. Genuinely the rare "a generic guide couldn't have written this" fact for Sendai's food identity, which is usually reduced to gyutan alone. ⚠ Confirm it's still open and check current hours locally — this pass couldn't re-verify hours directly.

Gyutan (grilled beef tongue), the non-touristy pick: Date no Gyutan Honpo, Aobajo — on the former Date-clan castle grounds, lunch-only (11:00–15:00), set meals from ¥2,330 — a named local food blogger's own favorite, distinct from the big station-area chains most visitors default to.

Kokubuncho, Bunka-yokocho & Iroha-yokocho — Sendai's drinking district and its retro Shōwa-era back-alley izakaya lanes, repeatedly named across independent sources as the city's "undiscovered by most visitors" nightlife core: tiny 8–10-seat bars in former storage-warehouse buildings. Genji Izakaya (a 200-year-old former warehouse building, local following) is one specific standout inside Bunka-yokocho — a good fit for the Nov 9 wind-down evening.
